Title: Over 80pct of haj depositors yet to meet RM15,000 savings threshold
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: More than 80 per cent of about 4.1 million depositors registered for haj have savings of less than RM15,000, which is the minimum amount required to maintain their current queue eligibility after the transition period ends.
Lembaga Tabung Haji (TH) said the figure indicates that while a large portion of depositors already have a haj queue position, they have yet to reach a sufficient level of savings in preparation for when an offer is extended.
Furthermore, 53 per cent of the total 9.8 million TH depositors have account balances of less than RM1,300, highlighting a significant gap between holding an account or queue position and being financially prepared.
"This figure points to an important reality, which is that many already have a haj queue position, but their savings have not reached the level required to make financial preparations when the time comes to perform the haj," TH told Berita Harian.
TH said the RM15,000 threshold is not a measure of wealth, but a basic benchmark of financial readiness based on the current minimum haj payment rate for the B40 group.
For depositors who have registered for haj, a transition period of more than two years is granted until Dec 31, 2028, to gradually increase their savings and retain their queue positions based on their original registration date and time.
Beginning Jan 1, 2029, depositors who have not reached RM15,000 will face a queue eligibility restructuring, and their positions will no longer depend solely on the registration date.
Existing principles remain unchanged.
The "first-come, first-served" principle is maintained among depositors who meet the minimum RM15,000 savings requirement, based on their respective haj registration date and time.
Depositors who complete the RM15,000 savings requirement on or after 2029 will regain financial eligibility for a queue position, but will not automatically recover their original queue placement.
TH confirmed there are no specific exemptions based on age, income group, or waiting period, including for senior citizens, the B40 group, or long-time registrants.
"TH is not seeking to deny anyone the opportunity, but to help establish a fairer, more orderly queue system that reflects the true readiness of prospective pilgrims," it said.
TH estimates that the implementation of Istito'ah could potentially reduce the waiting time from 147 years to around 68 years.
However, TH noted that the timeframe is only an estimate, as the actual position depends on the number of depositors who meet the savings requirement, Malaysia's haj quota, and current developments.
On Sept 11, TH launched the Haj Preparation Plan – Seruan Istito'ah, introducing automatic haj queue eligibility once a depositor's savings reach a minimum of RM15,000.
The new method replaces the existing registration and queue management process while retaining the "first-come, first-served" principle for those meeting the minimum savings requirement.

Title: HSIS Heart Centre handles 69 cardiac intervention cases in a single day
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Sultan Idris Shah Hospital (HSIS) Heart Centre in Serdang successfully managed 69 cardiology intervention cases in a single day on Friday.
The Health Ministry said the facility handled 45 per cent of all cardiac intervention cases across the ministry's 10 heart centres.
Operations typically run from 8am to 6pm, with all seven cardiac catheterisation laboratories (Cath Labs) fully operational to meet patient needs.
To clear the remaining backlog after office hours, four Cath Labs continued operating until late at night.
The high-intensity operations involved 80 healthcare personnel, including 14 cardiologists, six medical officers, 10 radiographers, eight assistant medical officers, and 40 nurses and healthcare assistants, the ministry said in a post on X today.
Of the total 69 cases, 40 were elective while 29 were emergency cases.
These included four Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (Primary PCI) procedures requiring rapid action to save heart attack patients.
The centre also demonstrated its expertise in handling complex coronary cases, performing 13 complex procedures using intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) imaging technology to ensure precise and safe treatment.
High-tech procedures carried out included four RotaPro Rotational Atherectomy cases and three Intravascular Lithotripsy cases.
The ministry added that both specialised procedures are designed for patients with cardiac blood vessels that are difficult to treat using conventional methods.
The ministry also expressed its appreciation to Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim for recognising the HSIS Heart Centre as a Health Ministry Cardiac Centre of Excellence (COE).
This achievement reflects the high commitment, efficiency, and teamwork of the entire HSIS Serdang cardiology team in ensuring patients receive fast, safe, and effective high-quality cardiac care, it added.

Title: Ed Sheeran set to return to stage after Palestinian controversy
Article:
PHILADELPHIA: Chanting protesters greeted concertgoers Saturday in Philadelphia ahead of pop superstar Ed Sheeran's first show since his tour plunged into turmoil ignited by his opening act's pro-Palestinian comments.
Rapper Macklemore was booted from Sheeran's US Loop Tour on Monday after the owners of stadiums hosting upcoming shows objected to his shouting "Free Palestine" onstage in New Jersey earlier this month.
Sheeran, 35, has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore, blaming the tour promoter.
Four supporting acts subsequently walked out on the "Shape of You" singer, issuing public statements citing their support for Palestinians.
Sheeran has been accused by critics of failing to stand up to the stadium owners – led by billionaire businessman Robert Kraft – and was targeted by boycott calls.
A few dozen pro-Palestinian protesters rallied outside a subway station near Lincoln Financial Field where Sheeran was set to perform Saturday night, waving Palestinian flags and chanting "Free, free Palestine."
Officers in a dozen police cars kept watch over the peaceful gathering from a distance.
Zach Roth, 28, selling CDs near the protest, said he felt bad for Sheeran because he will get criticized "either way."
At a time when a growing number of artists are speaking out against the conflict in Gaza and West Bank settler violence, the British performer has maintained his apolitical stance.
"I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them," he said Tuesday on Instagram.
However, he said, "those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum."
On Saturday, a pro-Palestinian group urged artists, fans and crew members to stay away from Sheeran's concerts.
"We now extend our call for boycotting Ed Sheeran's entire world tour, including the upcoming Latin American dates, and the as-yet-unannounced European leg," the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) said.
Solo show?
No new opening acts or backing bands have been announced, and it was not known how Sheeran planned to carry out his show Saturday.
The supporting acts that quit the tour included Sheeran's backing band as well as performer Finneas, who rose to fame collaborating with his pop superstar sister Billie Eilish.
Since Israel invaded Gaza in October 2023 following the worst attack on the country in its history by Hamas, the toll on Palestinians and the wider issue of Palestinian rights have emerged as a rallying cry in the entertainment industry.
From the Oscars to the Emmys, top music awards ceremonies and European film festivals, the Gaza war has frequently pushed its way onto the agenda.
The massive Israeli offensive in Gaza has left most of the territory in ruins and killed more than 73,800 people, according to the Gaza health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
On Saturday, Gaza authorities said the latest Israeli fire had killed at least four people.
On the resale market, tickets for the Philadelphia show have been changing hands at a slightly brisker pace since Monday when compared to previous dates on Sheeran's tour, according to tracking site TicketData.
The price of the cheapest tickets had fallen from US$123 on Monday to US$48 on Saturday evening, according to the site.

Title: Serian tops unhealthy air quality readings as 21 areas affected
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Twenty-one areas nationwide recorded unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings as at 8am today.
Based on data from the Malaysian Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS), three areas in Sarawak recorded the highest API readings — IPD Serian (182), Samarahan (168) and Sri Aman (164).
In Johor, two areas recorded unhealthy API readings — Larkin (162) and Pasir Gudang (155).
Meanwhile, Putrajaya, Nilai, Negeri Sembilan and Batu Pahat, Johor, recorded API readings of 154.
In Selangor, two areas — Shah Alam (153) and Johan Setia (127) — recorded unhealthy API readings, while Cheras was the only area in Kuala Lumpur to record an unhealthy reading, at 133.
Meanwhile, 41 areas recorded moderate API readings, including Batu Muda, Kuala Lumpur (99), Miri, Sarawak (99) and Politeknik, Kota Kinabalu (98).
Five areas recorded good API readings, including Tanah Merah, Kelantan (47), Sungai Petani, Kedah (41) and Alor Setar, Kedah (35).
For the record, API readings of zero to 50 indicate good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy and 301 and above hazardous.
Indonesia is battling its worst wildfires in more than a decade, with thick smog affecting millions of people and haze spreading to neighbouring countries.
Fires have been burning since last month across seven provinces on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, while dry weather and drought linked to a "Super El Niño" are making them harder to contain.
Smoke from the fires, containing soot and tiny suspended particles, has produced haze across parts of Malaysia and Singapore.
The wildfires could continue through October or early November due to a forecasted late rainy season.
Haze contains tiny airborne particles about 30 times smaller than a human hair. These PM2.5 particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and sometimes enter the bloodstream, experts said.

Title: #NSTviral: 'Mak Cik' impresses netizens with 4km run in 30 minutes [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A 73-year-old woman has impressed social media users after a video posted on Threads showed her running 4.07km in 30 minutes.
The post by @dausyusofjr showed her completing the run at a pace of seven minutes and 21 seconds per kilometre, drawing admiration from commenters who said they would struggle to keep up.
"Age 73. Is this pace okay?" the poster wrote in the caption.
The woman's name and her relationship with the person who shared the video were not immediately known.
The post has garnered more than 440,000 views and 22,400 likes.
View on Threads
Among those impressed was @farin.hashim, who compared the woman's performance with her own.
"That's fast. I cover 6km in an hour. She has already covered 4km in 30 minutes," she wrote.
Another user, @aufthority, joked that the woman could breeze through the Haj pilgrimage.
"She could complete all seven trips between Safa and Marwah in 15 minutes, God willing," the user wrote.
The New Straits Times has contacted the original poster for more details about the woman and the fitness routine that keeps her active at 73.

Title: Trump says will not tolerate attempts to slow AI growth
Article:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump on Saturday lashed out at critics of artificial intelligence and data centers, saying he would not allow the "destruction" of the industry and announcing the creation of a new government "AI Force."
Trump – who finds himself out of step with growing public skepticism over AI and dire safety warnings from AI industry leaders – said liberals want the "decimation, or destruction, of AI."
"I, as President of the United States, will not stand by and let this happen," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"
Trump added, without explaining, that he was creating an "AI Force" that would be tasked with "looking for BAD" actors, and would soon announce an AI coordinator or "Czar."
Trump's latest full-throated defense of artificial intelligence came even though polls show Americans are largely opposed to allowing the energy-guzzling data centers that are the engines of AI to be built in their communities.
As the war against Iran drags on and Americans grapple with the inflation it has fueled, Trump's approval rating is low.
Surveys suggest his Republican Party could lose control of the House and perhaps the Senate in November's midterm elections.
Trump is also firmly embracing the technology despite widespread warnings, even from top industry leaders, that AI development is going too fast and the technology could soon threaten our survival as ever-smarter AI agents escape the control of their human designers.
Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher who worked at Anthropic before resigning, set off the latest round of alarm by describing how those building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
Trump has repeatedly dismissed all the doomsday talk, calling it a "hoax" – a term he often uses for crises or issues he cannot control.
The president said the United States could not afford to lose a technological race with rival China and he insisted the only guardrails necessary were a "STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!"
In another social media post on Saturday, Trump mused on whether artificial intelligence is an accurate term, offered three alternatives in what he called a poll, and asked people to weigh in.
The three are superior intelligence, extreme intelligence and supreme intelligence, Trump wrote.
"This is a Poll, and I would appreciate everybody voting! Which is the best name for this ever growing "Revolution?"

Title: Bajau boat builder keeps lepa tradition alive
Article:
SEMPORNA: At 74, Biskal Mastal is keeping alive a Bajau boat-building tradition he learned from his father when he was 12.
The Kg Tonggulangan villager has built about 30 lepa boats, each taking about a year to complete and measuring about 11m long.
"It takes about a year to make one. There are many carvings. Its elaborate design also carries cultural meaning.
"Once you are skilled, you can do the carving by hand," he said when met during the inaugural Igal-Igal Festival held off Mantabuan Island here.
Semporna, on Sabah's southeastern coast, is a diving destination and gateway to islands such as Mabul and Sipadan.
The boats are made from red seraya wood, which can last for decades, even when used at sea.
[[nid:1536590]]
Biskal said the Bajau community once used lepa boats for fishing and travelling at sea, but they have since been replaced by modern speedboats.
Now, he builds the boats mainly for his own use and for Regatta Lepa, the annual celebration of Bajau culture and the traditional boat.
He said during cultural events and important community occasions, including khatam Quran ceremonies and other major gatherings, the boats are decorated with multi-layered flags and sail decorations known as sambulayang.
"The red colour on sambulayang represents courage, while yellow symbolises dignity or status.
"Lanterns serve as lights; they are must-have items on the boat."
Biskal's talent and patience in boat-making have borne fruit, with his work providing him with lucrative income of up to RM100,000 per boat.
[[nid:1536589]]
He also custom-makes miniature versions of the boats as souvenirs and said five full-sized boats are located in Putrajaya.
Despite the demand and the annual Regatta Lepa celebration, Biskal remains worried that the boat-making tradition could disappear as fewer people are interested in learning the craft.
"There used to be four of us who were skilled at making the boats, but I am the only one who is still alive.
"My youngest child is now learning it. But I also hope the government would encourage more people to learn it."

Title: UM121 start of a new chapter
Article:
UNIVERSITI Malaya (UM) will focus on improving its global standing while sustaining academic excellence, research and societal contributions as it marks its 121st anniversary, says Vice-Chancellor Professor Datuk Seri Dr Noor Azuan Abu Osman. While global rankings are not UM's sole focus, the university recognises their importance in shaping how higher education institutions are perceived internationally, he said.
"We recognise that rankings are important because the global community looks at a university through its ranking. We are working to improve UM's position beyond 56th globally in the coming years," he said after the launch of UM's 121st anniversary celebrations, known as UM121, at Dewan Tunku Canselor. "We will see the results when the Times Higher Education rankings are released soon, while the QS World University Rankings are expected next year."
The event, attended by more than 2,000 campus members, was officiated by Sultan of Perak Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah, who is UM chancellor. Present were pro-chancellors Toh Puan Datuk Seri Dr Aishah Ong, Tan Sri Datuk Zainun Ali and Tan Sri Datuk Seri Mohd Annuar Zaini.
Noor Azuan said UM's 121-year history carries a great responsibility to remain relevant to the nation and deliver tangible benefits to society. UM's history was closely intertwined with Malaysia's development, he said, having produced generations of scholars, leaders, and citizens, including six of the country's 10 prime ministers.
"UM121 is not merely about celebrating our age. It is about looking back at the history UM has built since 1905 and recognising our greater responsibility to ensure UM remains relevant to the nation. We want to advise the country to become better and, most importantly, create a real and meaningful impact for Malaysian society."
He said the university would build on its legacy through knowledge, expertise and research under the UM121 theme, "121 Tahun Kecemerlangan, Menyulam Masa Depan". "We want to continue this legacy by bringing forward our strengths in knowledge, expertise and research to create a greater impact, not only on society, but also on Malaysia and the world."
Noor Azuan added that UM recognised its responsibility to expand opportunities for all Malaysians. "We will do our very best for the nation's children by empowering knowledge, developing people, expanding opportunities and ensuring every step taken by UM continues to bring benefits to society and our beloved country," he said in his speech. He said UM's ultimate aspiration was to be recognised not only for academic excellence, but also for its research, people and character.
On technological transformation, Noor Azuan said UM was aligning its academic programmes and campus development with global advancements, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI). He said UM had played a significant role in Malaysia's development, including producing six of the country's 10 prime ministers. "We are aligning ourselves with global development. Academically, we are increasingly moving towards AI, with programmes and systems within UM developing alongside advancements in AI."
He said UM121 should also be viewed as the beginning of a new chapter rather than simply a celebration of the university's longevity. He said the university was inherited from previous generations and its present community had a responsibility to preserve it for future generations. "UM is not only owned by the UM campus community. It belongs to the people of Malaysia."
In his speech, Noor Azuan said the university's 121st anniversary should serve as a renewal of its commitment to the nation. "May this 121st year not be the culmination of the journey, but a new beginning for UM to continue serving, with knowledge strengthened and the nation honoured."
The UM121 celebrations will continue throughout the year through programmes highlighting the university's history, achievements, research and innovation, alumni and community contributions. The public and alumni can follow updates on the official website at um.edu.my/about-um121 and on Universiti Malaya's official social media platforms.

Title: Perkeso officer goes door to door to find those in need
Article:
WHEN most people are still turning over in bed, Muhammad Abrar Othman, or Abrar as he's better known, has already risen and started his day.
There are names to check, calls to make and addresses to find. Somewhere across Johor are people who have been injured, fallen ill or lost a loved one, and they may not even know that help is available.
Abrar's job is to find them.
A PERKESO Skuad Prihatin Sinergi officer, Abrar, 32, rises around 4.30am and is usually at his desk by 5.30am, going through cases that come in overnight.
He waits until after dawn to make his calls, mindful that there's little point waking up someone simply to tell them he's from PERKESO.
Some answer; some don't. For those who don't, he tries again — another call, perhaps a WhatsApp message, then another attempt around 8 or 8.30am.
By 9am, he's on the road. Johor is a big patch to cover. His work takes him to Kulai, Pasir Gudang, Kota Tinggi and Pontian.
Sometimes, he goes as far as Desaru, where the drive alone can take an hour and 45 minutes.
When I marvel at the early starts and distances involved, Abrar chuckles.
"I'm not working in Singapore. I work in Johor."
It's a throwaway joke, but it gives me my first glimpse of the man behind the job — easy-going and seemingly unfazed by the amount of road ahead of him.
Abrar has been with PERKESO for about 11 years, joining as a fresh graduate in his early 20s as an enforcement officer before moving to the benefits unit in 2018.
After the Movement Control Order at the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic, he was transferred to Skuad Prihatin Sinergi, taking him out of the office and into the homes of people who might otherwise slip through the cracks.
[[nid:1536529]]
He is also a two-time recipient of the Anugerah Khidmat Cemerlang PERKESO, in 2022 and 2025. But the awards are not what you notice when you're sitting with him in someone else's living room.
It's the way he settles into the conversation, the patience with which he lets people tell him what happened, and the fact that he rarely seems to be in a hurry to get through the paperwork.
WHERE TO BEGIN
Skuad Prihatin works on a simple principle: Search & Serve.
Rather than waiting for people to walk into a PERKESO office, its officers go looking for those who may not know they're entitled to assistance, or who may be too injured, ill, grieving or financially stretched to make the first move.
Cases come through hospitals, the police, community networks and even the media.
Once a name lands on Abrar's list, he starts tracking that person down — sometimes through phone calls and sometimes by driving for hours, following a trail to their latest address.
And when he gets there, the paperwork can wait.
Abrar sits down and talks to them first, asking what happened, about their family and work, and what worries them most.
Some are anxious and full of questions; others are upset or simply too overwhelmed to know where to begin.
But the business administration and marketing graduate lets them do the talking first. Only when they have settled down does he bring out the forms.
A visit can take an hour and a half, sometimes two hours. On an ordinary day, he may see two beneficiaries, although there are days when he manages five.
By 3 or 4pm, he's usually back at the office, handing the documents to the benefits team and flagging cases that need urgent attention.
The next day, he starts again. And that's how I came to spend a day following Abrar going from one modest house to another, meeting people whose lives have been knocked sideways by accident, illness and loss, and watching the man who came looking for them sit down and listen.
WHEN REZEKI COMES A-KNOCKING
At Sahbanah Saidali's modest single-storey house in Bandar Baru Kangkar Pulai, the rack outside the front door heaves with haphazardly arranged shoes and sandals.
Inside, glasses of water are waiting on the table, a small, almost instinctive gesture of hospitality.
Sahbanah, however, is hardly in a position to be playing host. The 49-year-old sits in a wheelchair, her headscarf neatly framing a tired face.
Her daughter moves around us, finding places to sit and tending to everyone while keeping a watchful eye on her mother.
For most of her life before her accident, Sahbanah was always on the move.
She has been working at Seagate Senai since 2011 as a material handler in the hard disk section, moving materials from one production line to another.
Almost an entire 10-hour stretch of her 12-hour shift was spent on her feet.
On her days off, she worked at a grocery shop, sometimes from 10am to 10pm. In a week, she worked four days at the factory, two at the shop and had one day to rest.
Her mornings began at 4.30am; she cooked, got ready and left home around 5.30am, often picking up a colleague along the way to work.
She has four children; her husband drives a lorry. It's a life built around keeping things moving.
Then came polling day. After voting in the Johor election in Tampoi and making a quick stop to shop, Sahbanah hurried home.
Her husband was washing the patio while she went inside to prepare food for her father. Even then, she was thinking about the next thing that needed to be done.
As she stepped out of the house, she glanced behind her.
The floor mat she expected to be in front of her was missing, but she didn't notice it. Her foot landed where she thought it would, but she slipped and twisted her leg as she fell.
Her husband, children and a neighbour's child rushed to her aid, but they could not lift her.
They had to bring out her mother-in-law's wheelchair to take her to the hospital. For a woman who'd spent most of her life on her feet, she now depended on a wheelchair to get around.
At first, doctors told her that her leg wasn't fractured, but the pain persisted. When a specialist reviewed the X-ray, Sahbanah was diagnosed with a soft-tissue injury with a suspected talus fracture and was put in a cast up to her knee.
She describes her injured leg as something that weighed 5kg.
For someone accustomed to an active lifestyle, she suddenly needed help to move from one room to another. Even getting to the bathroom meant relying on a walking frame.
"I felt completely helpless," she says.
The pain of not being able to walk again is one thing; the disruption to her life is even worse.
Sahbanah is still receiving her basic salary from Seagate, but she can no longer work at the grocery shop.
The bills and responsibilities, however, did not become lighter. Things she'd always taken care of were now being done for her.
Her husband would return around lunchtime with food; after 3pm, one of her children might come home with something to eat. Sahbanah would be there, waiting in her wheelchair.
She has never been comfortable asking her children for money. They're grown and working, but that didn't make it any easier to depend on them.
She spent too many years looking after everyone else and now, she has suddenly become the one who needed to be looked after.
"I was always rushing. Now, I wait," she says.
It's a simple sentence, but perhaps it captures better than anything else what the injury has taken from her.
HELP ARRIVES
When Abrar checked her PERKESO records, he found that she was an active contributor who had opted to enrol in LINDUNG 24 Jam, a scheme that provides protection for accidents that occur outside working hours.
Her medical leave ran from July 14 to Aug 19, and she received RM2,160.80 in temporary disablement benefit.
The payment came at a time when her grocery shop income had stopped, her independence had been curtailed and her family had suddenly taken on responsibilities she'd always carried herself.
As she confides about being unable to work and the fear of becoming a burden to her husband and children, her voice falters.
Her eyes fill with tears. Her daughter moves closer as Abrar reaches for the tissue box and gently places one in her hand.
When the payment came through within days, Sahbanah called it a rezeki — help arriving when the family needed it most.
She now has Abrar's number and messages him whenever she's unsure about something.
He arrived at her home as a PERKESO officer. Now, when she needs to know what comes next, she knows who to call.
"Sometimes, being a good listener is all that's needed," says Abrar.
WEIGHT OF UNCERTAINTY
At Lee Seng Kiong's house in Gelang Patah, the atmosphere is quieter.
It's another modest single-storey home in a housing estate, but with little furniture in the living room, it feels surprisingly spacious.
At the centre, a Chinese altar occupies pride of place, lending the otherwise uncluttered room a sense of permanence.
Clad in a crisp red-collared T-shirt, Lee, 59, welcomes us in, a bandage wrapped around his arm.
His wife pulls out red plastic chairs, taking one for herself and drawing it close to her husband.
[[nid:1536528]]
She stays beside him throughout, listening quietly as he recounts the accident that suddenly threw their household finances into uncertainty.
Lee makes his living from taking care of ornamental fish. He works at the Hong Ta Ikan Tropika fish farm in Pekan Nenas, where the job is physically demanding — there's always something to lift or move around.
These days, his right hand gets in the way of all of it.
He cannot straighten it fully. At night, a wrong movement can wake him with a jolt of pain. When it gets bad, he takes paracetamol and waits for it to subside.
His doctor told him there's no operation that can fix the problem. For now, he exercises the hand and takes care of it.
Even carrying water has become difficult. There's no pump at the fish farm, Lee explains, so he has to fill a container and carry it himself.
It's heavy — and it's his right hand he needs.
His accident happened on July 19, around 9am, along Km18 of the Johor Baru-Gelang Patah road.
He was riding his motorcycle when another motorcycle in front of him suddenly turned left. Lee had no time to avoid the motorcycle and crashed into it.
The impact left him with five broken ribs and injuries to his right hand, leg and head.
He spent five days receiving initial treatment at Sultanah Aminah Hospital before being transferred to Gleneagles Medini. He was given medical leave until Aug 21.
Asked when he expects to return to work, Lee says he doesn't know.
Fortunately, his boss has been understanding, telling him he can return when he feels ready and take on lighter jobs instead of the heavy work.
For now, that takes some pressure off. But Lee is the sole breadwinner. His wife has stopped working, and without knowing when he can resume his usual duties, he has no idea how long the household can manage on what they have.
Which makes a decision he made a few months earlier all the more significant.
Lee had heard about PERKESO's new 24-hour protection scheme from his boss, but he wasn't immediately convinced.
He has heard the stories about the difficulties in making a claim — that the process took a long time and it was full of red tape.
This was reinforced by his own experience years earlier. At that time, while working at a motorcycle workshop, a tyre exploded and struck him in the head.
The workshop boss told him not to bother making an insurance claim; it would be difficult and he wouldn't get much anyway.
So, Lee didn't make a claim.
This time, when the new LINDUNG 24 coverage came up, he asked his children what they thought of it.
Keep it, they told him. If something happens outside work, at least there'd be some protection.
So, he kept it.
Then, on July 19, something did happen. PERKESO's records showed that Lee was an active contributor who qualified for coverage for accidents occurring outside working hours.
For his medical leave from July 19 to Aug 21, he received RM1,604 in temporary disablement benefit.
[[nid:1536527]]
It wouldn't replace everything that Lee could earn, but for a sole breadwinner, it offered some relief to his family as he recovers from his injury.
Abrar also helped him make sense of what comes next. Lee wanted to know what to do with his medical certificate, what would happen if he needed another and whether physiotherapy would be covered, particularly when each session could cost RM200 or RM300.
Abrar patiently guided him on what help was available and what he needed to do.
"He really explains everything," Lee says, turning to the PERKESO officer, who smiles modestly.
For now, Lee still has an injured hand, a long recovery ahead and a household waiting for him to get back on his feet.
Now, I understand why Abrar says the visits can take so long. You can't simply walk into someone's home, collect a set of documents and leave.
There's always a story before the paperwork.
In Sahbanah's case, it's the loss of independence; in Lee's case, it's the fear of losing the household's only income.
And in Kavita Rajagopal's predicament, the story is more tangled.
PIECING HER LIFE BACK TOGETHER
Kavita's two-storey rented house sits among the modest homes in a residential area.
Inside, the house suggests a busy family life — people coming in and going out, doors opening and closing — the ordinary buzz of a lived-in home.
However, there's very little of that now.
The living room is sparsely furnished, with a single table standing in the otherwise open space.
We sit together on a rug on the floor, close enough that the conversation soon feels less like an interview and more like Kavita slowly confiding how her life has unravelled.
The room is dim, the afternoon light muted by makeshift curtains. Upstairs, several rooms stand empty.
Until recently, she rented the rooms to sub-tenants for extra income.
It was a precarious arrangement for her as the anchor tenant, but it helped make the numbers work — until she was assaulted by one of her tenants during a confrontation over the rent.
The 42-year-old has spent about a decade working as a security guard at a factory in i-Park Senai, putting in 12-hour shifts from 7am to 7pm.
Her salary is about RM2,500, but after deductions and an advance, she takes home around RM1,800.
With RM1,400 going towards the house rent, there's little left for everything else.
On July 5, at about 11.30pm, Kavita went upstairs to collect rent from one of her tenants. Instead, the tenant became aggressive and she found herself under attack.
Her son arrived soon after and was also injured in the confrontation, requiring eight stitches to his injuries.
When the situation escalated, Kavita stepped in between her son and the tenant and was struck on the right hand, fracturing her middle finger.
She was taken to Temeng­gong Seri Maharaja Tun Ibrahim Hospital for treatment and her hand became swollen and stiff, with numbness and pain when she tried to move it.
For someone whose livelihood depends on turning up for a 12-hour shift, an injured hand is more than an inconvenience.
It threatens her ability to earn. Her salary has already gone unpaid for a month and her employer is waiting for her to recover, while the RM1,400 rent continues to fall due.
[[nid:1536526]]
Yet when Kavita talks about the future, she doesn't dwell on any of that for long.
She talks about work. She has even driven with one hand because she needs to get around and, perhaps more importantly, because she cannot bear to be completely still.
"I just want to return to work," she says.
She wants her old routine back — the 7am start, the long shift, the tired journey home, the monthly salary that allowed her to pay the bills and look after herself and her son.
It wasn't an easy life, but it was one she knew how to manage. Her 22-year-old son drives a school van when he can.
At one point, he was staying with a friend because he didn't have the money or transport to manage on his own.
Kavita worries about him even as she tries to keep her own life from slipping further out of reach.
She's also worried about the house. She told her landlord she had fallen because she did not want to risk losing the home she was struggling to pay for.
Upstairs, bloodstains can still be seen on the floor, which hasn't been completely cleaned since the confrontation.
Her dog died in March and she lives alone now. There's a lot for Kavita to carry, but she doesn't seem to want anyone to do it for her.
What she wants is the chance to get back to doing what she has always done: working, earning and looking after herself and her son.
BREATHING SPACE
PERKESO wasn't on Kavita's mind when it happened. She only learnt about the organisation's 24-hour protection scheme when a clerk-friend told her she could make a claim.
When Abrar was asked to follow up on her case, he went to the address listed on her identity card in Taman Universiti. But Kavita no longer lives there.
So, he kept looking. Eventually, he found her at the current home. By then, her claim was already moving through the system.
PERKESO records showed Kavita was an active contributor who had agreed to coverage under the Skim Keselamatan Bukan Bencana Kerja (SKBBK) LINDUNG 24 Jam.
She was placed on medical leave from July 17 to Aug 24 and received RM1,528.80 in temporary disablement benefit.
By the time of our visit, she had also received RM600 in assistance. With a take-home pay of around RM1,800, minus the monthly rent of RM1,400, the money offered some breathing space while she recovered.
But Abrar's role didn't end with the payment. He talked Kavita through the medical certificates she needed to keep track of, what would happen next and where she could turn if her recovery took longer than expected.
He and his colleague, Andi, also discussed whether Social Synergy could connect her to other forms of social assistance or employment support.
There were limits to what PERKESO could do. It couldn't make her hand heal faster or replace the salary she lost.
But people like Abrar could ensure she did not have to navigate what came next entirely on her own.
And perhaps that's why the extra mile that he went to look for Kavita really matters.
Kavita had no permanent place to stay, and the details on her MyKad were not up to date.
Abrar could have just stopped looking for her with the outdated details. But he didn't. He kept looking until he found her.
Now, sitting together on the rug in that dim living room, he listens as Kavita talks about her injured hand, her son, the rent, the salary she has missed — and again about work.
For Kavita, work is more than a job. It's the thread holding her life together, and the thing she's most desperate to get back.
TO SEEK AND TO SERVE
This, says Abrar, is what Skuad Prihatin is about: to search and to serve.
After a day following him from one house to another, the phrase takes on a more human meaning.
It means going looking for people who might otherwise fall through the social security net — getting into the car and driving across Johor, calling again when nobody answers, or sometimes waiting until after dawn because a family has not yet been told that a loved one has died.
And when he finally reaches the right door, the work is rarely as simple as collecting documents and ticking boxes.
There's always a person behind the case: someone frightened, angry, embarrassed or simply exhausted; someone who may not know what they're entitled to, or who's wary of a process they've never dealt with before.
Abrar has learned that sometimes the most useful thing he can offer at the beginning is simply his time.
For all the weight of the work, there's nothing particularly solemn about the man himself.
He still makes time for football, badminton and the gym, laughs readily about the early starts and long drives, and seems almost amused by the fact that he's awake before dawn while most of us are still asleep.
But beneath that easy humour is an understanding that every address on his list belongs to someone whose life has been knocked off course.
He cannot mend Sahbanah's broken leg, make Lee's ribs heal faster or put Kavita's missing salary back in her hands.
But he can show up at the right door, at the right time, when someone's life has been knocked off course. Sometimes, that is where helping begins.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Old photo, Facebook search reunite friends after four decades [WATCH]
Article:
PETALING JAYA: Two friends separated for four decades have been reunited, thanks to an old photograph and a search on Facebook.
When Devaki Rani Munusamy and Rohani Ambri, both 73, met recently, they held onto each other tightly, promising never to lose touch again.
Their friendship began in 1969 in Segamat, Johor, over shared meals at the school canteen during recess.
"Every week, we would eat and spend time together. Once school ended, we went our separate ways, but we still spoke to each other whenever we could," said Devaki Rani.
Life soon took them down different paths.
Rohani married young in 1970 and started raising a family, moving frequently as her husband, Mohammad Ropee Adman Yahyauddin, was posted to different military bases.
[[nid:1536616]]
Devaki Rani, meanwhile, went abroad in 1974 to study hairdressing and beauty before returning home and marrying in 1979.
"After (Rohani's) marriage, she came to see me a few times and we went shopping. She was already driving by then," said Devaki Rani.
"Then I went abroad to study for about two years, and we lost touch. I don't know how, but I managed to send my wedding card to her. She came to my wedding.
"After the wedding, we were all busy. I went my way, she went hers."
Devaki Rani later moved between Johor Baru, Terengganu and Kedah as her husband completed his medical housemanship.
There were no mobile phones to bridge the distance then, no landline numbers or forwarding addresses to follow. Gradually, the two friends drifted out of each other's lives. But Rohani was never forgotten.
"I used to look at crowds in shopping centres and wonder, 'Is Rohani here?' But I knew I wouldn't recognise her after all these years.
"It was only recently, while looking through my old photo album, that I told my son: 'This is my friend Rohani. I've been thinking about her. I want to find her, but I don't know how'."
That old album would eventually provide the thread that led them back to each other.
Devaki Rani's second son, Dr Madhusudhan Shanmugam, had been chatting with his mother when she pulled out an old photograph to show him how much she resembled her grandchildren.
As they flipped through the album, they came across a photo from Rohani's wedding.
"I told my mum that I could help her find Rohani, but since her name is quite common, it wasn't easy," said Dr Madhusudhan.
"Then my mother told me that Rohani's husband's name was Ropee. I asked ChatGPT for help, and it said the uniform he was wearing looked like that of a paratrooper.
"When I searched 'paratrooper Ropee', there was an article about one 'Captain Ropee', with a small name tag beside his photo. I compared the photos, and it was the same person."
Further searches led him to social media profiles he believed belonged to Ropee's children.
Ropee had died recently.
He sent a message on Facebook to one of the sons with the question: "This may sound strange, but are you by any chance Captain Ropee Adman's son?"
The reply quickly opened a door that had been closed for decades.
"When I mentioned that my mum had been looking for her friend, within 10 minutes, her son sent me her phone number.
"I called Rohani and said: 'Hold on, Auntie, I'm handing the phone to my mum.' At first, my mother was puzzled because they look so different now.
"Then Rohani spoke up: 'Hello, my old friend, Devaki.' I told her: 'Mum, it's your friend, Rohani!' She immediately stood up, went to her room and started chatting."
Four decades of silence had ended with a phone call.
When the two women finally met again recently, the years apart gave way to a tight embrace.
Devaki Rani, who stays in Klang, has four children while Rohani has six.
For Devaki Rani and Rohani, their coming together again was a dream come true.
"We are very happy to meet each other again after so many years," said Rohani.
"Once in a while, I used to wonder, where was Devaki? I didn't expect this reunion after 40 years."
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Cuba works to restore power after another blackout
Article:
HAVANA: Cuba worked Saturday to restore power after its seventh major blackout of the year, as the communist-run island grappled with woes triggered by a US fuel blockade.
This latest nationwide outage, the 12th since late 2024, occurred after a failure in transmission lines paired with "unstable weather conditions," state-run utility UNE said Friday.
The blackout first hit five provinces in eastern Cuba, including Havana, and then spread to the rest of the country.
UNE said 48 percent of its customers in Havana had regained power on Saturday.
"The re-establishing is being done gradually, as conditions permit," it said on X.
In the last blackout in early August it took the company 36 hours to get the lights back on fully.
The island of over nine million people endures constant power cuts due to the poor state of its aging thermoelectric plants.
But the situation has worsened significantly since January, when Washington imposed a de facto energy blockade on the island in a bid to pressure Havana's communist government.
A severe lack of fuel makes it difficult to supply Cuba's power plants and backup generators, which typically run on imported diesel.
"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez, who was just finishing up her workday, told AFP on Friday.
"Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy," the visibly irritated 36-year-old added.
In recent weeks, blackouts have lasted more than 30 hours in the capital, while in outlying provinces, they have sometimes stretched past 60 hours.
The cuts have also affected the island's water supply and mobile phone network, and general living conditions are extremely tough for residents.
Havana blames the crisis on an array of US-imposed punitive measures, while Washington attributes the hardship to poor internal management.
An economic crisis has engulfed the Caribbean island, where 66 percent of the population lives in poverty, according to an independent study released this week.
That is compared to 45 percent in mid-2025, with rising food costs behind the sharp increase in poverty, the research by the Christian Center for Reflection and Dialogue (CCRD) suggests.
The findings give "an indicative picture that the problem is growing," study coordinator Mayra Espina told AFP.
Another retiree, Zunilda Garcia, took the latest blackout in stride, stepping outside to charge a small lamp with solar energy.
"We have to wait and stay calm," Garcia, 60, said. "We can't lose hope."
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: 'UM must continue building on legacy'
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Universiti Malaya (UM) must continue building on its legacy by expanding its national impact, adapting to student needs and nurturing future leaders, according to alumni and current students.
UM chief of staff Maheran Zainal Abidin said the institution had evolved significantly since she graduated from the Faculty of Economics and Administration in 1999.
"From the time I studied here until now, there have been tremendous changes. The developments have been widespread and have aligned closely with student needs," said the 50-year-old alumnus.
Maheran, who returned to serve her alma mater at the Office of the Vice-Chancellor, said her passion for education and desire to give back inspired her decision to return.
"I find the education system to be very dynamic. I wanted to give back to my alma mater.
"I hope my contributions, however small, can support UM's growth and excellence."
On UM's achievements, including reaching the 56th spot on the QS World University Rankings, Maheran expressed pride in the institution's progress while noting room for further growth.
"As an alumna, I hope UM will continue moving forward because this university shapes future generations."
She added that visibility remains essential, provided it yields tangible benefits for the country.
"UM needs to be more visible, but in a way that creates a real impact on the nation."
She highlighted the strong support network of the university's estimated 300,000 alumni, facilitated by the Alumni Centre.
"The support from our alumni has been very encouraging. With solid alumni backing, UM will become even stronger."
[[nid:1536351]]
For third-year biotechnology student and chief facilitator of Kolej Tun Syed Zahiruddin, Nurin Alysya Nazrul Hizam, 21, her connection to UM began in childhood.
She recalled her mother bringing her to the campus and encouraging her to pursue her studies there.
"She told me this was a great place and that many prominent figures studied here. From a young age, I set my heart on attending UM."
She said her experience at UM went beyond academic education, particularly her involvement in student leadership.
"UM is the oldest and the top university in Malaysia. I hope UM remains No. 1 and continues to produce leaders capable of making their mark"
First-year Science Foundation student Isaac Chang, 18, said moving from Kota Kinabalu, Sabah, to UM allowed him to experience a diverse student community.
"I chose UM because of its diverse community. I get to interact with people from different states and countries."
He said his positive campus experience had reinforced his intention to complete his degree at UM.
"I am very grateful for the opportunity to study at UM. I look forward to continuing my studies here."
He said the university's 121st anniversary marked an opportunity to attract students seeking quality education and holistic skills development.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Haze leaves food delivery riders working through health risks
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Food delivery riders are forced to keep working through the haze despite health risks as limited occupational safety guidance leaves many with little choice but to carry on.
North-South Initiatives executive director and co-founder Adrian Pereira said riders who fell ill or were unable to work due to the poor air quality may have no guaranteed compensation, making it difficult for them to simply stop working.
"The real question is, do they really have a choice or not? If they are sick or they cannot ride, there is no guaranteed compensation."
Pereira said the lack of clear guidance was concerning as prolonged exposure to haze could affect workers in ways that might not be immediately apparent.
"The danger is that we do not know and we are not sure what to do next."
He added that his organisation, through partners including Gabungan E-Hailing Malaysia (GEM) and Transformasi Pengangkutan Awam Darat (TPAD), had been advising gig workers on occupational safety and health, and urging delivery platforms to share responsibility for workers' well-being.
For rider Muhammad Riezwan Ishak, 30, the haze has made it difficult to focus on the road as his eyes become irritated while making deliveries around Teluk Intan.
"My eyes get a bit itchy, so I cannot focus too much on the road while making deliveries," he said.
Riezwan Ishak, who is also short-sighted, said the haze had further affected his visibility, prompting him to wear black sunglasses while riding, although they offered limited relief.
He said he continued accepting orders but would ride more slowly when the haze became severe and inform customers that their food might take longer to arrive.
"Customers place more orders when haze conditions worsen, as they avoid going outdoors.
"I just make sure I wear a face mask and inform customers that I will deliver the order very slowly so that I do not have a high risk of getting sick due to the haze."
For part-time food delivery rider Muhammad Zaki Abdul Rahim, 26, the haze has been felt in his breathing.
Zaki, who has asthma, said he had experienced chest tightness and difficulty breathing since the haze began, forcing him to use his inhaler more frequently.
"I rarely used my inhaler before this, but now I use it more frequently, around three to four times a week."
Zaki limits his exposure by waiting indoors at food vendors, petrol stations and shopping malls between deliveries.
He said the haze had not significantly affected his income as he could usually reach his part-time delivery target, but he remained concerned about its effect on his health.
Delivery rider Mohd Amirul Hakim, 31, meanwhile, has reduced his working days and shifted to night deliveries as he struggles with persistent coughing.
"I work on alternate days now. I have been coughing badly and continuously because of the haze, so I work only as much as I can manage."
Amirul said the haze also caused eye and throat irritation and affected visibility on the road, requiring him to ride more carefully.
He also preferred working at night to avoid the combination of daytime heat and haze.
The riders said wearing masks, limiting time outdoors, taking shelter between deliveries and adjusting their working hours were among the ways they tried to reduce their exposure while continuing to work.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Thousands protest inaction over climate crisis in Switzerland
Article:
LAUSANNE: Several thousand people marched in the Swiss cities of Geneva and Lausanne on Saturday to protest government inaction in the face of global warming.
They were answering a call by a coalition of more than a hundreds of associations and political parties under the common banner: "No 50-degree summers!"
People of all ages took part in the marches, carrying placards with slogans such as "No Planet B" and "We're cooked!", AFP journalists noted.
The larger demonstration was at Lausanne, where organisers said at least 8,000 had taken part.
One marcher, 31-year-old union activist Guillaume Matthey told AFP he hoped this was the start of "a new cycle of widespread popular mobilisation" to put pressure on the country's political and financial leaders for their lack of response to the climate crisis.
Already in 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Switzerland was not doing enough to fight climate change – the first time an international court ruled against a country on this matter.
"This is about telling our authorities that it's really the time to act," said one marcher in his 60s, Yves Froidevaux.
"We can't just finance weapons and then not care about the rest of it – that's not on," he added.
"There's been a real lack of water this summer," said Vincent Fontannaz, a 47-year-old actor dressed up as a giant drop of water.
"It's not just about swimming pools, it's most of all about agriculture – and for our survival in fact," he added.
One marcher, 55-year-old architect Laurent Guidetti, wore a gas mask made out of plastic bottles. He was one of the lucky ones to have a well-insulated apartment "that stays cool at night", he said.
This summer however, he had thought about people who were not so lucky. "It's going to be very tough for them," he added.
And even if they got through this summer's heatwaves, he did not know how they would manage against the higher temperatures expected in future summers.
After Saturday's demonstrations, other protests have been called in several Swiss cities in the coming weeks until October 2.
Switzerland's summer heatwaves forced the closure of a nuclear power station and caused record low water levels in Lake Zurich.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Bersatu urges RoS to decide on complaint against PN soon
Article:
PETALING JAYA: Bersatu hopes the Registrar of Societies (RoS) will decide soon on a complaint filed by the party last month over alleged breaches by Perikatan Nasional (PN) leaders.
Bersatu president Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin said the party had raised eight key matters which it claimed had been violated or disregarded by PN leaders.
"Party secretary-general Datuk Seri Mohamed Azmin Ali was called to provide an explanation on the matter.
"We lodged the complaint and, following the meeting, we found that RoS was taking the matter seriously.
"We leave it to RoS' discretion and hope a decision can be made soon," he told reporters at Bersatu's 10th anniversary celebration here today.
RoS had previously confirmed receiving a formal complaint from Bersatu over the party's alleged exclusion from a PN Supreme Council meeting on July 16.
Pas president Tan Sri Abdul Hadi Awang was previously reported to have said Bersatu's membership in PN had automatically lapsed after Muhyiddin announced the formation of a new coalition.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Muhyiddin: Pas decided to end political cooperation with Bersatu
Article:
PETALING JAYA: Pas decided to end its political cooperation with Bersatu, said Bersatu president Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin.
He said the decision had formally ended political cooperation between the two parties within Perikatan Nasional (PN).
Muhyiddin stressed that the decision was made entirely by Pas, led by Tan Sri Abdul Hadi Awang, and was not initiated by Bersatu.
"Pas made the decision not to continue cooperating.
"This was not Bersatu's choice (to end the cooperation)," he told reporters at Bersatu's 10th anniversary celebration here today.
On June 9, Pas officially ended its political cooperation with Bersatu with immediate effect.
The decision was made at a special meeting of the Pas Central Working Committee after considering reports, studies and assessments of the current relationship between the two parties.
The meeting endorsed a decision by the Pas Syura Ulama Council on June 2 concerning the policy, religious and public-interest considerations of Pas' political cooperation based on the principle of Muslim unity.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Muhyiddin denies acquittal linked to talks with PH
Article:
PETALING JAYA: Bersatu president Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin has denied that his acquittal on four charges involving RM200 million was linked to efforts to forge cooperation with Pakatan Harapan (PH) to form a new political alignment.
He said the High Court's decision had nothing to do with any efforts to cooperate with PH.
"Instead, it involved court proceedings over the charges I faced.
"The trial involved clear and specific charges which, as of today, were unfounded.
"Therefore, the prosecution withdrew the charges against me and I was acquitted of four of the seven charges," he told reporters at Bersatu's 10th anniversary celebration here today.
Muhyiddin said he did not see how the decision could be linked to cooperation with PH.
The High Court on Sept 15
acquitted and discharged
Muhyiddin of one charge of using his position to obtain RM200 million in gratification and three money-laundering charges involving the same amount.
The prosecution had applied for a discharge not amounting to an acquittal, but the court instead granted a full acquittal.
High Court judge Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin said the prosecution had not provided reasons for discontinuing the four charges and exercised the court's discretion in Muhyiddin's favour. He still faces three charges of abuse of position involving RM25.3 million in alleged bribes.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Muhyiddin: Bersatu has held talks with several parties on new political alliance
Article:
PETALING JAYA: Bersatu president Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin has confirmed that the party has held talks with several political parties on efforts to form a new political alignment and chart its direction for the 16th General Election (GE16).
However, he said no decision had been finalised as discussions were still ongoing.
"Bersatu is open to exploring cooperation with other parties that respect the basic principles of Bersatu's struggle.
"I can say generally that meetings with several political parties have taken place. I have mentioned extending invitations to meet and discuss," he told reporters at Bersatu's 10th anniversary celebration here tonight.
Muhyiddin said Bersatu could not favour any particular party when determining the form of cooperation for a new political alignment.
He said since its establishment, Bersatu had maintained that it could not move on its own and needed cooperation with other parties to strengthen its political position.
"We were tested when we contested alone in the Negri Sembilan election, and that experience proved our position on the importance of cooperation was correct.
"However, Bersatu was denied cooperation by Perikatan Nasional (PN), particularly by PAS within PN, and that was what happened," he said.
Muhyiddin said the formation of PN was previously aimed at creating a clear political coalition to strengthen the position of the parties involved.
"When the election came, we contested and won. That's how it works.
"However, Bersatu has no choice if there are parties that decide not to continue the cooperation," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Education Ministry aims to strengthen Korean language skills among students
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Education Ministry aims to strengthen Korean language proficiency among students in the country under its international language subject initiative.
Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek said students in Malaysia had shown strong potential in learning Korean.
"Every year, the Education Ministry sends students to Korea, while Korean teachers also come to Malaysia to teach our students.
"They communicate in English and use translations, so we see a need to improve their Korean language skills," she said in her speech at the dinner marking the 100th anniversary of Kuala Lumpur Technical Secondary School (TIKL) here today.
Also present were Education Ministry Technical and Vocational Education and Training Division director Zulkernain Fauzi, TIKL principal Ahmad Nazryshah Mohamed Khalid and Alumtek Kuala Lumpur president Norhisham Soin.
TIKL is among nine technical secondary schools (SMT) nationwide that have been rebranded as Technical Fully Residential Schools (SBP-T).
The other eight are SMT Alor Setar in Kedah, SMT Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra in Penang, SMT Tuanku Jaa'far in Negri Sembilan, SMT Bukit Piatu in Melaka, SMT Kuala Terengganu in Terengganu, SMT Kuantan in Pahang, SMT Johor Bahru in Johor and SMT Sejingkat in Sarawak.
Meanwhile, Fadhlina announced a RM150,000 contribution to TIKL to assist with maintenance of the school.
She also launched the TIKL 100 Years coffee-table book produced specially to mark the anniversary.
The dinner brought together more than 1,000 alumni from various generations.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Health ads that breach rules to be referred to MCMC, says Fahmi
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Complaints about online health advertisements and promotions that may breach regulations or mislead the public will be referred to the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) for review and further action.
Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said the issue was among those raised during his meeting with representatives of medical associations and healthcare experts here today.
"The matter will be referred to MCMC for review and further action with the relevant parties," he said in a Facebook post.
He said the meeting was held to hear views, suggestions and concerns from the representatives and medical experts.
Fahmi also expressed appreciation for the open and constructive discussions, saying insights from those directly involved were important to help understand the issues on the ground and find more effective solutions.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Bersatu will not go solo in GE16, says Muhyiddin
Article:
PETALING JAYA: Bersatu will not contest the 16th General Election (GE16) on its own, but will instead move as part of a political coalition, its president Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin said.
Muhyiddin said any decision taken by the party must be based on its principles and interests.
"Almost everyone who gave me their views said Bersatu cannot move alone. Yes, I agree with this view.
"We must move as part of a political coalition," he said in his speech at Bersatu's 10th anniversary celebration here today.
Muhyiddin said in deciding on coalition partners, Bersatu must choose those who respect the party's struggle and value its contributions.
"Most importantly, (they must be) partners whose principles and aspirations are aligned with those of our party," he said.
He said among Bersatu's key principles was to build a developed, prosperous country free from kleptocratic practices, as well as a progressive and democratic nation that respected the rights of the people enshrined in the Federal Constitution.
"This includes forming a country that protects the special position of Malays and Bumiputera, the sanctity of Islam, as well as the legitimate rights of all races," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Sirim's NEW TDM Project to advance digital manufacturing
Article:
SHAH ALAM: Malaysia's tool, die and mould (TDM) industry is set to enter a new phase of digital transformation and global competitiveness with the launch of  NEW TDM Project next month.
Implemented under the 13th Malaysia Plan and the New Industrial Master Plan 2030, the initiative aims to strengthen the TDM ecosystem through digital engineering, talent development and advanced manufacturing capabilities.
The project builds on capability and capacity gains achieved under TDM 2.0, which ran from 2022 to this year, and is expected to help TDM companies move further up the manufacturing value chain.
This will help firms develop more sophisticated tooling solutions and compete more effectively in regional and global markets.
Sirim president and group chief executive officer Nik Sazali Nik Hussin said TDM 2.0 laid a strong foundation for the industry, while the NEW TDM Project would accelerate its transformation.
"Our ambition is to move beyond 'Made in Malaysia' towards 'Designed, Engineered and Made in Malaysia'," he said at the Appreciation Nite and Award Presentation for the TDM 2.0 Project on Friday.
The NEW TDM Project will focus on three  areas: a digital platform for 3D design based on the 3DEXPERIENCE platform; talent development covering 3D design, digital engineering, CAD/CAM/CAE and advanced manufacturing; and, capability development aimed at strengthening the ability of companies to deliver advanced tooling solutions.
"Through these initiatives, the project seeks to support the progressive development of TDM companies, from preferred suppliers to original equipment manufacturers, to strategic suppliers for Tier 1 companies and ultimately to globally recognised TDM solution providers."
On TDM 2.0, Nik Sazali said the programme concluded a significant phase of industry development, with 36 beneficiary companies completing its three core components, covering coaching and certification, design capability development and equipment acquisition.
TDM 2.0 delivered measurable improvements across participating firms. Overall, 88 per cent of the companies increased their production capacity, recording an average surge of 164 per cent.
A total of 77 per cent reduced their overall lead time, achieving an average reduction of 29 per cent.
The programme also supported product diversification, with 70 per cent of participating companies introducing new product lines, averaging an increase of 12 product lines per firm.
The participating companies contributed RM292 million in gross value added in 2024 alone.
Nik Sazali said that TDM was
not merely a supporting industry, but a core industrial foundation on
which manufacturing capability was built.
"A country may attract an automotive plant, an aerospace manufacturer, an electronics factory or a medical device producer.
"But if the critical tooling, dies and moulds required by those industries continue to be designed, engineered and manufactured somewhere else, then a significant portion of the value chain remains outside the country."
He added that localising TDM capabilities was essential to capturing greater economic value within Malaysia.
"It is not localisation for localisation's sake.
"It is about capturing more value in Malaysia, strengthening our domestic supply chains, developing Malaysian engineering capability and creating higher-value jobs for Malaysians."

Title: Diana revelations, Harry return give Charles a testing week
Article:
Britain's King Charles faces a trying few days, from screaming headlines raking over reportedly cruel comments about his late ex-wife Diana to his errant son Harry re-entering public life at an event in London.
Britain's monarch was hosting some of the world's biggest names in artificial intelligence in Scotland on Thursday, urging them to find a way forward that would protect humanity.
But nearly all Britain's newspapers splashed their front pages with details from a soon-to-be-released book by Diana's brother that quotes Charles as saying in the days after her death in 1997: "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough."
In response, Buckingham Palace issued an unusually pointed statement: "His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."
The Daily Mail, which is serialising the book, said on its website: "King at war."
The Daily Telegraph said "Palace hits back at Diana's brother," on its front page, while the Sun said: "Recollections may vary... again," in reference to a previous royal response to criticism from Harry and his American wife Meghan.
The book, written by Earl Charles Spencer about his sister Diana, who died aged 36 in a Paris car crash, pursued by photographers, is being published on Tuesday.
Reactions from the public ranged from apathy to outrage.
"You can't give oxygen to an argument that ultimately is nonprovable," said James Taylor, a 41-year-old sales executive in London, adding that Spencer's claims could be viewed cynically as being about selling copies of the book.
But Terrie Sechrist, a 68-year-old lawyer, felt the reported remarks reflected badly on the king.
"(Diana) was his wife and the mother of his children. I just don't know anyone with a heart that would say that."
The publication comes as Harry, and possibly Meghan, prepare to attend a number of charitable events in the coming weeks.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their two children returned to live in Britain last month, six years after stepping down from royal duties and moving to the US, from where they regularly criticised the royal family.
The return was a surprise even to close family, with Harry's father, the king, only being told days before the news became public.
Harry and his brother, heir-to-the-throne Prince William, are also barely on speaking terms.
Seeking to prevent any confusion, the palace wrote to British officials to state that the king's youngest son and his wife were not working royals, and should be treated as private citizens with commercial and charitable interests.
A spokesperson for Harry and Meghan said they were surprised by the move.
At the same time, the palace is still grappling with major issues that could shape the future of the British monarchy.
King Charles' younger brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office over his ties to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The royal family are also facing increasing questions over their wealth, and polls show that younger people are not overly interested in the institution.
The writer is from Reuters

Title: Keep subsidies for consumers in Budget 2027, says ministry
Article:
BATU KAWAN: The Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry hopes allocations for subsidies, consumer affairs and the people's well-being will continue to receive due attention in the 2027 Budget, despite fiscal challenges arising from the rising cost of fuel subsidies.
Minister Datuk Armizan Mohd Ali said the allocations were important to enable the ministry to carry out its responsibilities effectively, particularly in ensuring the stability of supply and prices of goods.
He said the ministry hoped subsidy allocations, including those for the Subsidised Diesel Control System (SKDS), cooking oil and the Price Standardisation Programme for Sabah and Sarawak, could be maintained.
"Most importantly for us now, amid such major challenges, is to ensure that consumer subsidies can be maintained.
"For example, this year alone, under the 2026 Budget, only RM15 billion was actually allocated for fuel subsidies, but now the fiscal space that needs to be used for fuel subsidies has almost reached RM40 billion.
"That is an increase of almost threefold. So, that is one of the challenges," he told reporters at the closing ceremony of the 2026 Jom Malaysia Festival at Batu Kawan State Stadium here today.
Armizan said the ministry had submitted its applications and several key areas for consideration by the Finance Ministry (MOF) under the 2027 Budget, taking into account current needs and the country's fiscal capacity.
However, he said the government's targeted subsidy reforms had enabled subsidies to continue reaching eligible groups despite rising costs.
He said mechanisms such as SKDS and Budi Diesel enabled fuel subsidies to continue reaching eligible groups, while the subsidised packet cooking oil programme could also be maintained despite higher crude palm oil (CPO) prices.
Armizan said the ministry would continue working with MOF and relevant ministries to ensure allocations were utilised optimally and in a targeted manner while delivering direct benefits to the people.
Meanwhile, he said the cost-of-living issue cut across various ministries and would also be addressed at the National Cost of Living Action Council (NACCOL) meeting chaired by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim on Sept 29.
He said the eight NACCOL clusters would give the ministries involved an opportunity to propose new initiatives or recommendations to strengthen existing measures to address cost-of-living issues.
